passage: When Saurabh arrived in the small town of Hanagal as the new co-op officer, everyone liked him. He remembered names, brought sweets for the office and praised Sangeeta's accounts on his first day. By the third month, things had shifted. He expected the best chair at every meeting and his tea brought to his desk first. When the co-op's farm-loan scheme won praise from the district, he took the stage alone, though Sangeeta had designed it. When she mentioned her mother was in hospital, he said, "Yes, yes, anyway, about my report." He could still be warm, but mostly when the district officer was visiting.

qa.q: Who designed the farm-loan scheme?
qa.a: Sangeeta designed it.

qa.q: What does Saurabh's "Yes, yes, anyway, about my report" suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests he shows little interest in Sangeeta's feelings and cares mostly about his own work and image.

qa.q: What turning point shows the change in Saurabh, and what does it cost the office?
qa.a: Taking the stage alone for a scheme Sangeeta designed showed his charm turning into credit-taking, which leaves colleagues feeling used.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel when he brushes off her mother's hospital stay?
qa.a: She probably feels hurt and unseen, and may start to resent his early compliments.

grounding: A charming new officer comes to expect special treatment, takes credit and shows little interest in a colleague's feelings unless it serves him.

passage: When Amara moved into the Toronto flat, Nour thought she'd found the perfect flatmate. Amara cooked jollof for the whole building, laughed at every story and called Nour "my sister" within a week. By winter, the pattern was clear. Amara used Nour's laptop without asking because her own was "too slow for important things". She told their friends the house party had been her idea, though Nour had planned every detail. When Nour cried after a bad job interview, Amara glanced up from her phone and said, "You'll be fine. Did you see what my boss said about my presentation?" Only when Amara needed a favour did the old warmth come back, sudden and bright.

qa.q: What did Amara cook for the whole building?
qa.a: She cooked jollof.

qa.q: What does Amara's reply after Nour's bad interview suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests she feels little concern for Nour's hurt and turns the attention back to herself.

qa.q: What turning point showed Amara's charm had changed, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Taking credit for the party Nour planned showed the charm had turned into entitlement, making the friendship one-sided.

qa.q: How might Nour feel when the old warmth comes back only when Amara needs a favour?
qa.a: She probably feels used and confused, unsure which Amara is real.

grounding: A charming flatmate comes to expect special treatment, takes credit and shows interest in her friend only when it serves her.

passage: In her first month at the design studio in Manchester, Amara was everyone's favourite: coffee for the team, compliments on every sketch, stories that made the manager laugh. By month four, things were different. She expected the corner desk by the window, and got it. She presented Soo-ah's packaging idea to the client as "something I've been developing". When Soo-ah mentioned her mother was in hospital, Amara said, "Oh no," then asked if Soo-ah could still finish the mock-ups by Friday. Amara was warm when the director was around and bored when she wasn't. She told herself she was simply more ambitious than the others. The team had stopped inviting her to lunch; she hadn't noticed yet.

qa.q: Whose packaging idea did Amara present as her own?
qa.a: Soo-ah's.

qa.q: How does Amara seem to feel about her own behaviour?
qa.a: She seems pleased and self-satisfied, telling herself she is simply more ambitious, with no sign of guilt.

qa.q: What could Amara do if she wanted to repair things with the team?
qa.a: Credit Soo-ah openly, ask how Soo-ah's mother is and stop expecting special treatment.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah feel when Amara asks about the mock-ups right after hearing about the hospital?
qa.a: Soo-ah likely feels hurt and used, as her worry is brushed aside for deadlines.

grounding: Shows a charming newcomer who begins to expect special treatment, takes credit and shows little curiosity about others' feelings.

passage: In his first week as team lead at the logistics firm, Tarun won the floor over: he remembered birthdays, ordered samosas for everyone and told stories that made meetings fly. By the third month he'd decided that people who liked him this much wouldn't mind a few favours. He left early on Fridays and expected the team to finish his reports. In the quarterly review he presented Suraj's route-planning sheet as his own. When Suraj asked about it later, Tarun looked puzzled. "We're a team, yaar. Why so touchy?" When Suraj asked for two days off because his father was ill, Tarun sighed about deadlines and didn't ask how his father was. The next day, with the director visiting, Tarun spoke warmly about "caring for our people".

qa.q: Whose sheet did Tarun present in the quarterly review?
qa.a: Suraj's route-planning sheet.

qa.q: What was Tarun thinking by the third month?
qa.a: He felt smug and entitled, believing people who liked him wouldn't mind doing favours for him.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Tarun treated his team, and what could fix it?
qa.a: He took credit and ignored feelings; crediting Suraj and asking about his father would start to fix it.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel hearing Tarun talk about caring for people?
qa.a: Suraj likely feels bitter and resentful, since Tarun showed no care when his father was ill.

grounding: Illustrates a charming lead who grows entitled, takes credit and shows empathy only when it serves him.

passage:
Tenzin,
Long time! You'll be happy to hear things are going brilliantly here in Dubai. The bosses love me; I'm basically running the branch. Listen, I need a small favour. I'm coming to Delhi next month for a conference and will need your flat for four nights. You won't mind sleeping at your sister's, right? Also, could you pick me up from the airport at 2 a.m.? Oh, and I saw something on your page about your father's surgery. Hope that went fine. Anyway, I'll send the dates. Remember how I always made our college trips fun? You owe me a few of those.
Wasim

qa.q: How many nights does Wasim want the flat?
qa.a: Four nights.

qa.q: What does Wasim seem to expect from Tenzin?
qa.a: Wasim seems smug and entitled, assuming Tenzin will give up the flat and do airport pickups without being asked properly.

qa.q: What would a more caring letter from Wasim include?
qa.a: Real questions about Tenzin's father and life, and a request that leaves Tenzin free to say no.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel reading "Hope that went fine. Anyway"?
qa.a: Tenzin may feel hurt and used, since the father's surgery gets one line before more demands.

grounding: Shows a charming person expecting special treatment from a friend while showing little curiosity about the friend's feelings.

passage:
Honestly? The first month at the agency was perfect. I'm Jyoti; everyone loved me. I brought samosas, remembered birthdays, made the boss laugh.
But after that, I figured I'd earned a bit of room. When Salma pitched the festival campaign idea in our small meeting, I polished it and presented it upstairs as mine. She'd never have sold it the way I did.
Now she's sulking. Last week she tried to tell me about her mother being in hospital, and I kept checking my phone. I mean, I asked the right questions when her brother turned out to know the client. That's just smart.
And now people say I've "changed". I haven't changed. I just expected them to appreciate me, and they stopped. I'm a little resentful, if I'm honest. Why is it always about their feelings?

qa.q: What idea did Salma pitch in the small meeting?
qa.a: The festival campaign idea.

qa.q: How does Jyoti feel about people saying Jyoti has changed?
qa.a: Jyoti feels resentful and unappreciated, believing special treatment was earned, and asks why it is always about their feelings.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Jyoti treats Salma, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Jyoti took credit for Salma's idea and showed interest only when it was useful; giving Salma credit and listening without an angle could start to repair it.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Salma when Jyoti kept checking the phone?
qa.a: Salma likely felt hurt and dismissed, sharing her mother's hospital stay only to be ignored after her idea had been taken.

grounding: Shows a charming newcomer who comes to expect special treatment, takes credit and shows interest in others' feelings only when it is useful.
